title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
titleZh: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
author: Kotlopou
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。

summaryRaw: I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that!

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)1/2+o(1). The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!). All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

comments.author: nickysielicki
comments.textRawHtml:
I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography.

For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big.

Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that.

That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet.

Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

children.author: gjskngnf
children.textRawHtml: I’m not confident I’d say that open weight models can achieve frontier performance given 10x the tokens. Most of the cutting edge math discoveries we’ve seen were achieved using internal models the public still doesn’t have access to. Roughly, math discoveries come from compute*intelligence and we have little insight on how intelligent their unreleased models are. We also have little info on how much compute they spent to achieve their results. Therefore, it’s hard to decouple the two. However, since the general math community seems to be relegated to doing verification as opposed to discovery despite being able to crowd source compute, that leads me to believe that the frontier labs really do have a special sauce.

children.author: torginus
children.textRawHtml:
Potentially quite far - a lot of math results were proven using specialized models trained to do math and theorem proving, while very likely skipping training on more general stuff like how to deploy an SPA or put together a scenic tourist route.

I'd say the average person like me would have time appreciating their capabilities, meanwhile they'd be quite lacking in basic skills.

I guess the improvements are somehow gated and rolled into public models eventually.
